description: We are farfromoffice, a team of independent developers from Türkiye. Our interests include software engineering, game development, simulations and mostly open-source technologies. We aim to combine our technicall skills and our creativity to develop innovative solutions for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Margin is a space mission design game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. The player takes on Wildfire Watch: keep a small Earth observation satellite sending fire data home for 30 days. They choose the instrument, solar array, battery, radio, pointing system, ground stations, orbit and launcher while live margins track mass, budget, power, downlink and storage. Before launch they predict what will limit the mission. Then they watch the launch in 3D, fly the satellite through eclipses, ground station passes and random failures, and read a report that explains with numbers why the mission met its goal or fell short.

Orbit periods, eclipses and ground contact windows come from NASA GMAT runs, the ground stations are NASA Near Space Network sites, and the Earth is drawn from NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery. Every number in the game carries its source and is labelled documented, approximation or fictional.

Students rarely get to run a whole mission from concept to operations, so engineering trade-offs stay abstract. Margin turns them into choices you can feel and test again: every gram, watt and megabit counts and a failed mission teaches as much as a successful one.
details:
What it does?
Margin walks the player through a full small satellite mission in one loop: briefing, design, prediction, launch, operations, report. The Design screen follows the NASA mission segments (launch, space, ground, user). The game blocks launch if mass, budget, orbit or structure size do not fit, and warns about power, downlink, memory and pointing. During the 30-day mission the player changes camera on-time and radio use and handles live failures such as battery fade, a lost solar string or a frozen radio or camera that a restart can clear. The report compares the prediction with what actually limited the mission and puts the last two flights side by side.

How it works
The spacecraft is simulated in 60-second steps: solar power in sunlight and eclipse, battery charge, Normal and Safe mode, data made by the camera, stored onboard and sent home during ground station passes. Orbit periods, eclipse fractions and contact windows for three orbits (ISS-like 400 km, SSO 550 km, SSO 700 km) and three NASA Near Space Network stations (Svalbard, Alaska Satellite Facility, Wallops) come from NASA GMAT R2025a runs. Component masses and powers come from real CubeSat vendor datasheets. Failure rates follow published CubeSat reliability studies. Costs and some rates are teaching values and are labelled fictional. We checked the model against hand calculations and GMAT (for example 92.6 min period and 38.3 % eclipse at 400 km), and a balance sweep flew all 15,120 launchable designs: 21 % meet the goal, UHF radio never does, and a pointing system more than doubles the success rate.

Benefits and impact
Players learn by failing safely: a design that looks fine on paper runs out of battery in eclipse or fills its memory because the radio is too slow. Predicting the limit before launch, then seeing the real one, builds intuition for systems engineering. The game needs no account, runs offline on Linux and Windows, and is open source under MIT so teachers and students can read and change the data.

Creativity
Margin turns budget sheets into a playable mission. Instead of a score alone, the player gets an explanation: which margin broke, when, and why. A short 3D launch from the pad to the spacecraft unfolding in orbit connects the numbers to a real feeling of flying a mission.

Tools
Godot 4.7 with GDScript (Compatibility renderer), GUT for automated tests, NASA GMAT R2025a with a Python generator for orbit data, plain HTML, CSS and WebGL for the website (its globe reuses the game's Earth shader), GitHub Actions for builds and Pages.

What we considered
Accuracy versus clarity: we simplified on purpose (no drag, heat, link budgets or attitude dynamics) and say so in game and in RESEARCH.md. Data honesty: every value has a source and a provenance label. Accessibility for beginners: plain language tooltips, units explained, and difficulty choices for failures.
